pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 7–9; ice in different forms and states of matter — sea ice forms when salty ocean water freezes (salty, relatively thin); glacial ice forms from snow compacted over centuries (fresh, very thick); icebergs break off glaciers and float in the sea. Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (vapour), and salt lowers water's freezing point.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS2 Y4 'States of matter' (solid/liquid/gas; freezing and melting at specific temperatures; the water cycle).
• Standards—US: NGSS 2-PS1-4 earlier; 5-PS1-1/-3 (matter and its properties); links to MS-PS1 particle model.
• Operational details: two threads — (1) states of matter and the freezing/melting change, and (2) telling apart three polar ice types by ORIGIN (frozen seawater vs compacted snow vs calved glacier). The surprising, testable fact is that salt LOWERS the freezing point, so seawater freezes below 0°C — investigate by freezing salty vs fresh water and comparing. Distinguish sea ice (from the ocean) from glacial ice/icebergs (from land snow) because it matters for fresh vs salt water and for sea level later.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (7) name the three states of water; Tier B (8) explain that salty water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water; Tier C (9) classify sea ice, glacial ice and an iceberg by where each came from (frozen sea vs compacted snow).
bestPractices: Run a fair test: freeze salty vs fresh water and observe the salty sample needs to be colder to freeze, evidencing salt lowers the freezing point
Separate ice by ORIGIN not just appearance — sea ice (frozen ocean, salty, thin) vs glacial ice/iceberg (compacted snow, fresh, thick)
Use the particle-ish idea lightly: freezing/melting is the same water changing state, not a new substance
Connect to the water cycle so the three states link to evaporation, precipitation and meltwater
Foreshadow the sea-level idea: melting SEA ice barely changes sea level, but melting LAND ice (glaciers) adds water — a hook for later years
keyRepresentations: State-change strip: ice → (melt) → water → (evaporate) → vapour, and reverse
Salty-vs-fresh freezing comparison with a thermometer showing the lower freezing point
Three-ice classification chart by origin (sea / glacier / iceberg), salt, and thickness
commonMisconceptions: All ice is the same — sea ice, glacial ice and icebergs differ in origin, saltiness and thickness
Seawater freezes at 0°C like fresh water — salt lowers the freezing point, so it freezes colder
Icebergs are frozen seawater — they calve from glaciers, so they are compacted snow and fresh, not salty
Ice and water are different substances — they are the same water in different states
Melting sea ice raises sea level a lot — floating sea ice barely changes it; land ice melting is what adds water

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: ice comes in different forms and water exists in three states. Learners investigate that dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point (seawater freezes below 0°C, near about -1.8°C) and classify polar ice by ORIGIN: sea ice (frozen ocean, salty, relatively thin) vs glacial ice (snow compacted over centuries on land, fresh, very thick) vs icebergs (chunks calved from glaciers, so fresh land-born ice). Water exists as solid (ice), liquid (water) and gas (vapour), and ice/water are the same substance changing state. A hands-on fair test and sorting-by-origin tasks anchor these ideas, with a later qualitative hook to how melting floating sea ice vs land ice affects sea level differently.

activities.title: Fair test: does salt change the temperature at which water freezes?
feedback: If a learner predicts both freeze at the same temperature, point to their recorded observations, for example if the salty sample was still liquid when the fresh one had frozen, or its thermometer reading was lower when ice first formed.
If a learner thinks salt warms the water, note that the salty sample actually has to reach a colder temperature before it freezes — salt is lowering the freezing point, not heating anything.
Reinforce the fair-test logic: because only the salt changed, the difference in freezing must be caused by the salt.
activities.rationale: A controlled comparison makes an invisible property (freezing-point depression) observable and lets learners reason from their own evidence rather than being told. KS2 Y4 expects observing changes of state at specific temperatures.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils compare and group materials by state (solid/liquid/gas), observe changes of state at specific temperatures, and study the water cycle
Dissolved salt depresses the freezing point of water, so seawater freezes near -1.8°C; sea ice is frozen ocean water while glacial ice and icebergs derive from compacted snow on land
learnerActions: Set up two samples: one fresh water, one salty water (e.g. with a measured spoon of salt stirred in).
Use the same amount of water, the same type of container and the same starting temperature, and place both in the same freezer/cold spot so the test is fair — only the salt differs.
Observe which freezes first, and if a thermometer is available, record the temperature at which each turns to ice.

Record what you actually observe. Fresh water normally freezes at about 0°C; salty water usually stays liquid longer and must get colder before it starts to freeze (with a lot of salt it may not freeze at all in a home freezer).
State the conclusion in your own words: salt lowers the temperature at which water freezes.
activities.intendedInsight: Dissolved salt lowers water's freezing point, so seawater must get colder than 0°C before it freezes — the two samples differ only because of the salt.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain with salt on ice
feedback: If the prediction is 'salt just warms/melts ice, so it gets warmer', contrast it with the observation that the mixture actually became colder.

If the prediction is 'nothing happens', point to the comparison: if the salted cube melted faster than the unsalted one, or its thermometer reading dropped below 0°C while plain melting ice stayed near 0°C, the salt changed something.
Praise reasoning stated before observing, since naming the expectation first makes the surprise meaningful.
activities.rationale: Eliciting a prior reason surfaces the common 'salt just melts/warms ice' intuition so the contrary observation can confront it; the road-salting link transfers the concept to a familiar context.
sourceClaims: Dissolved salt depresses the freezing point of water, so seawater freezes near -1.8°C; sea ice is frozen ocean water while glacial ice and icebergs derive from compacted snow on land
learnerActions: Before touching anything, PREDICT and give a reason: will sprinkling salt on an ice cube make it warmer, colder, or do nothing?

Sprinkle salt on one ice cube and leave a second, unsalted cube beside it for comparison, then OBSERVE: compare how quickly each melts and, if possible, read a thermometer in each (the salted mixture can drop below 0°C while plain melting ice stays near 0°C), watch for frost on the outside of a metal cup, or touch the cup only briefly to feel it getting colder.
EXPLAIN what happened: salt lowers water's freezing point, which is why the salted ice-and-water mixture can sit below 0°C and why the sea must get colder than 0°C before it freezes.
Connect to everyday life: explain why people scatter salt on icy roads and paths in winter.
activities.intendedInsight: Salt lowers the freezing point; this is the same idea behind seawater freezing below 0°C and behind salting icy roads.

activities.title: Sort the three ices by where they came from
feedback: If a learner says 'icebergs are frozen seawater', remind them icebergs calve from glaciers, so they are compacted snow and fresh.
If a learner treats all ice as identical, ask them to trace each piece back to the sea or to land snow.
Confirm correct sorting by having the learner justify each placement with its origin, not its look.
activities.rationale: Classifying by origin targets the 'all ice is the same' misconception and prepares the fresh-vs-salt distinction that matters for later sea-level reasoning.
sourceClaims: Dissolved salt depresses the freezing point of water, so seawater freezes near -1.8°C; sea ice is frozen ocean water while glacial ice and icebergs derive from compacted snow on land
learnerActions: Examine three ice examples (or labelled cards/cross-sections): frozen ocean water, compacted mountain-glacier snow, and an iceberg that snapped off a glacier.
For each, decide its ORIGIN (ocean vs land snow), whether it is salty or fresh, and whether it is thin or very thick.
Place the iceberg with the glacial/land-born group and explain why: it calved from a glacier, so it is compacted snow — fresh, not salty.
Build a short classification chart: sea ice = frozen ocean, salty, relatively thin; glacial ice = compacted snow on land, fresh, very thick; iceberg = broken-off glacier, fresh and usually thick.
State the key idea aloud: not all white ice is the same — it can come from the salty sea or from freshwater land snow.
activities.intendedInsight: Polar ice is distinguished by origin, not just appearance; this determines whether it is salty or fresh.

activities.title: The same water in three states
feedback: If a learner says ice and water are different substances, point to melting and refreezing the same sample to show it returns.
Link each state change to a familiar water-cycle event to reinforce it is one water moving between states.
activities.rationale: Addresses the 'ice and water are different substances' misconception and meets the states-of-matter and water-cycle standards.
sourceClaims: KS2 Y4 pupils compare and group materials by state (solid/liquid/gas), observe changes of state at specific temperatures, and study the water cycle
Students investigate properties of matter and changes of state
learnerActions: Trace the state-change sequence: ice melts to water, water evaporates to vapour, and the reverse (vapour condenses, water freezes).
Explain that ice and liquid water are the same substance in different states, not different materials.
Connect the three states to the water cycle (evaporation, precipitation, meltwater).
Give one example of each state of water from everyday life.
activities.intendedInsight: Freezing and melting change water's state, not its identity; the same water can be solid, liquid or gas.

activities.title: Which melting ice changes the sea level? (foreshadowing)
feedback: If a learner says melting the floating sea ice will raise the sea like a glacier would, remind them the floating ice is already sitting in (displacing) the water.

Encourage connecting this back to the sorting task: ice still sitting on land (glaciers) adds water to the sea when it melts or slides into the sea; once an iceberg is already floating, its melting barely changes the level, just like sea ice.
activities.rationale: Introduces the land-ice vs sea-ice sea-level distinction at an age-appropriate, qualitative level as a hook for later climate topics, targeting the conflation misconception. No source claim directly establishes the displacement/sea-level principle, so none is cited.
learnerActions: Compare two cases: a chunk of ice already floating in the sea, and ice sitting on land (a glacier).
Predict what happens to the water level when each melts.
Reason it through: floating sea ice already displaces its own water, so melting it barely changes the level; land ice adds new water to the sea when it melts.
State why this distinction matters when thinking about how melting ice affects the ocean.
activities.intendedInsight: Melting floating sea ice barely changes sea level, whereas melting land ice adds water and raises it.

constraints: The salt-and-water freezing investigation needs an actual comparison (salty vs fresh) under fair-test conditions; a thermometer makes the freezing-point effect measurable but is ideally-available, not strictly required. Without one, learners can still observe which sample freezes first and whether the salty sample is still liquid when the fresh one has frozen. This is only an indirect sign, so keep amount, container and starting temperature the same.

Labelled cross-sections and tap-to-reveal state-change strips clearly present the categories but do not let a learner experience salty water staying liquid at 0°C; use them alongside, not instead of, the investigation.

Sorting cards and matching tasks can teach and check whether a learner classifies ice by origin, but do not by themselves build or elicit the freezing-point intuition or a spoken explanation; reserve them as a companion to the hands-on work.
The sea-level comparison is a qualitative age-appropriate hook, not a quantitative treatment; keep it to 'barely changes' vs 'adds water'.
Keep the particle idea light at this age: freezing/melting is the same water changing state.
Icebergs float because ice is less dense than liquid water — note this if the floating/density point arises, so 'floats' is not confused with 'made of frozen seawater'.
Observing the salt-on-ice mixture: for ages 7–9 the salt-ice mixture can get very cold, so keep contact brief and prefer reading a thermometer or watching frost form on a metal cup.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; all source claims are marked verified:false in the original and have not been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original listed seawater's freezing point near -1.8°C but the recommendation said 'well below zero'; -1.8°C is only slightly below 0°C. For ages 7–9 the robust takeaway is 'colder than 0°C', so activities avoid asserting a large depression and treat a home-freezer comparison as qualitative.

A simulated 'drag a temperature dial until it freezes' interaction was described in the original; it is retained as an optional way to present the fair test, not a required mechanism, and real freezing of two samples is preferred where feasible.
The claim that 3D 'adds no explanatory power' was a catalog fit judgement, not an established pedagogical law; omitted rather than propagated.

Density as the reason icebergs float appears in the stated learning evidence but was underdeveloped in the recommendation; added to constraints for accuracy, not made a central activity since the focus is origin and freezing point.

The sea-level foreshadowing activity relies on a displacement principle not covered by any of the three source claims (which address states of matter, changes of state, and ice origin/freezing only); it is offered as a qualitative hook with no source cited and should be treated as unverified.

assess.poeTask: Give the child an ice cube, some salt and (ideally) a thermometer. Ask them to PREDICT, reason first, what salt sprinkled on the ice will do — make it warmer, colder, or nothing — many say 'salt melts ice, so it warms it' or 'nothing'. They add salt and OBSERVE the ice melting AND the temperature dropping below 0°C (or the mixture feeling colder / frost forming outside a metal cup). Then EXPLAIN: salt lowers water's freezing point, which is also why the salty sea must get colder than 0°C before it freezes. The pre-observation reason exposes the 'salt just melts/warms ice' intuition.
probeDeeper: Where does glacial ice come from, and why does that make it fresh, not salty?
Why do people scatter salt on icy roads and paths in winter?
If you melted a floating chunk of sea ice in a glass of water, would the level rise a lot? What about ice sitting on land?
How can the very same water be a solid, a liquid and a gas?
assess.correctAnswer: No. Sea ice forms when the ocean freezes — it's relatively thin and comes from salty water; glacial ice forms from snow compressed over centuries on land — it's fresh water and very thick, and icebergs are chunks that break off glaciers and float out to sea. And salt water does NOT freeze at the same temperature as fresh: salt LOWERS the freezing point, so seawater must get colder than 0°C before it freezes. Water can also be solid (ice), liquid (water) or gas (water vapour).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All ice is the same' — no distinction between sea ice and glacial ice.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort by origin: sea ice = frozen ocean (salty, thin); glacial ice = compressed snow on land (fresh, thick); icebergs = broken-off glacier.
errorPatterns.distractor: Ice is just ice — sea ice and glacier ice are exactly the same thing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats sea ice and glacier ice as identical; can't say where each comes from.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Salt water freezes at the same temperature as fresh (0°C)' — unaware salt lowers the freezing point.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Demonstrate/explain: salt lowers the freezing point, so the sea must get colder than 0°C to freeze (why we salt icy roads).
errorPatterns.distractor: Salty seawater freezes at exactly the same temperature as fresh water.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts seawater freezes at 0°C like fresh water.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Melting sea ice raises sea level the same as melting glaciers' — conflates floating sea ice with land ice.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Floating sea ice already displaces its water (level barely changes); LAND ice (glaciers) adds new water and raises the sea. This distinction returns in climate topics.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says melting the floating sea ice will raise the sea like melting a glacier would.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks all ice is the same and salt water freezes at 0°C like fresh.
responseLevels.full: Separates sea ice (salty, thin, frozen ocean) from glacial ice (fresh, thick, compressed snow) and icebergs (calved glacier), knows salt lowers the freezing point, and can reason about states of matter and the land-vs-sea-ice sea-level difference.
responseLevels.partial: Distinguishes sea from glacial ice OR knows salt lowers the freezing point, but not both, or muddles the sea-ice/land-ice sea-level effect.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: There are two kinds of ice near the poles: sea ice (frozen seawater) and glacial ice (from snow squashed down over centuries), and icebergs break off glaciers. A student says 'ice is just ice — it's all the same frozen water, and salty seawater freezes at the same temperature as fresh water.' Is all polar ice the same, and does salt water freeze at the same temperature as fresh? Explain the differences.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the 'ice is ice' idea can't distinguish sea from glacial ice or predict the salt effect; a student with the concept separates them by ORIGIN (sea vs compressed snow) and knows salt lowers the freezing point. Two documented misconceptions are targeted at once, so guessing right is hard.
